I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

vignette:
Four months ago, Amir was working late, debugging a stubborn block of code on the forty-second floor. He remembers the low rumble that started deep beneath his feet, a sound he felt in his teeth before he truly heard it. Then came the violent lurch. His monitor flew off the desk, and the world outside his window became a sickening, tilted blur of sky and neighboring buildings. In the moments that followed, a cacophony of groaning steel and shattering glass became the entire universe. Amir recalls the darkness, the dust choking his lungs, and a single, repeating sound of a high-pitched alarm from somewhere down the hallway, a sound he can still summon with perfect, terrifying clarity. The sequence of events after the main collapse remains a chaotic fog in his mind; he cannot say for certain how long he was trapped before the shouting of rescue workers broke the silence.

The initial gratitude for his survival has long since curdled into a pervasive sense of dread. Amir has come to believe he is fundamentally and permanently altered. "I used to be a happy person," he stated flatly in his first session, "but now I am always miserable." He obsesses over his decision to stay late that evening, a choice he now views not as professional diligence but as a catastrophic personal failing. This conviction that somebody else would have known better, would have gone home and avoided the situation entirely, has become a cornerstone of his current worldview. It fuels a deeper, more corrosive belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore, as if he used up all his luck in that collapsed office tower. This constant self-reproach seems to summon the trauma; telling himself he should have known better makes the memory of the collapse feel more immediate and accessible, as if it is waiting to provide evidence of his failure. This pervasive sense of personal deficiency and a foreshortened future keeps his threat system on a constant, hair-trigger alert.

This heightened sense of threat now dictates the entire geography of his life. At his open-plan office, the unexpected movement of a colleague walking past his desk is enough to make him jolt with adrenaline, his body reacting as if the floor is once again about to give way. This physical startle response often rips a memory from the past into the present, and for a few disorienting seconds, he is back in the rubble, the smell of concrete dust sharp in his nostrils and the wail of that alarm screaming in his ears. The experience feels so utterly real that he has to grip his desk to orient himself. As a result of these sensory ambushes, Amir now lives his life by a set of rigid, unspoken rules. Before sitting down in any room-a conference room at work, a restaurant, even his own living room-he must first identify all possible exits. This constant planning is exhausting, but it feels like the only rational way to navigate a world he now perceives as fundamentally unstable. Feeling this afraid all the time has become the most convincing proof he has that his life has changed beyond repair; his body's constant state of alarm quietly confirms the thought he works hardest to resist-that this is simply who he is now. The constant feeling of being in danger primes him to notice any potential threat, which in turn makes it more likely that an innocuous sound or movement will trigger another vivid, fragmented memory.

The intrusive memories are the most tormenting aspect of his days. When one breaks through, his immediate response is to fight it. He will retreat to the men's room and engage in a frantic, silent argument with himself, forcing himself to list only positive thoughts: his wife's name, a successful project, the taste of a good meal. The effort is immense and rarely successful. At other times, particularly after a near-miss in traffic or the sudden sound of a siren, he finds himself lost in long, looping ruminations about who was to blame-the building inspectors, the construction company, the city itself-a desperate attempt to channel his terror into a more manageable anger. This struggle to control his own mind only seems to confirm his belief that he is broken beyond repair.

His strategies for managing his distress have begun to poison his life. His wife, Layla, has noticed he flinches with alarm now whenever she touches him unexpectedly on the shoulder. He sees the hurt in her eyes, which only adds another layer to his conviction that he has lost the capacity for happiness. The forced positivity he attempts feels like a lie, and its constant failure to bring relief reinforces his sense of being permanently damaged. This, in turn, makes him feel even more vulnerable and on edge, tightening the loop between his thoughts and his physical state of alarm. He has actively avoided a follow-up medical appointment for injuries he sustained, as the thought of a hospital-with its sterile smells and urgent sounds-is too closely tied to the immediate, terrifying aftermath of the disaster. It was after Layla found him standing motionless in their dark kitchen for nearly an hour, paralyzed by the sound of a passing ambulance, that she told him she was scared for him. That was when Amir finally made the call, driven by the fear that his internal world was not just collapsing, but taking his marriage and his future down with it.

  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
